Part 1 · Fundamentals

What decides how much liquid a centrifugal pump delivers into this system?

Part 1 · the plan

Five ideas that fix the flow

  1. Headwhy pumps are rated in metres, not in kPa
  2. Pump curve and system curvewhat the pump offers and what the pipework demands
  3. Operating point, speed and valvewhere the two curves cross, and how to move it
  4. Power, current and NPSHwhat it costs, and when the pump starts to cavitate
  5. Two pumps in parallelhow flows add, and why each leg has a check valve

1 · Head

Head is pressure expressed as a height of liquidstep 1 of 2

$H$
head: energy per unit weight of liquid
m
$p$
gauge pressure
Pa
$\rho$
liquid density (gas oil 870)
kg/m³
$g$
gravity, 9.81
m/s²
$$H=\dfrac{p}{\rho g}$$

For this gas oil 1 m of head = 870 × 9.81 Pa ≈ 8.53 kPa.

Interactive — same head, different liquid

Why pump curves are drawn in metresstep 2 of 2

From the previous slide$p=\rho g H$
pressure rise across the pump

An impeller gives every kilogram the same energy whatever the liquid, so the head stays fixed while the kPa rise scales with density.

1 · Head

Total head carries three forms of energy

$v$
mean liquid velocity in the pipe
m/s
$z$
elevation above a datum (pump centreline)
m
$$H_{tot}=\dfrac{p}{\rho g}+\dfrac{v^2}{2g}+z$$

Bernoulli: pressure, velocity and elevation head.

In 3-inch lines at 14 L/s, v²/2g is about 0.4 m — small beside 32 m.

2 · Pump curve

How the impeller makes head

  • Liquid enters the eye and is flung outward by the vanes.
  • The volute slows it down: velocity turns into pressure.
  • With the discharge shut, the pump still makes its highest head, the shut-off head.

2 · Pump curve

The pump curve: head falls as flow rises

$\Delta H$
head added by the pump (discharge − suction)
m
$H_0$
shut-off head at full speed, from the vendor test
m
$Q$
flow through the pump
L/s
$k$
curve coefficient fitted to the test points
m/(L/s)²
$s$
speed as a fraction of 3600 rpm
—
$$\Delta H=H_0\,s^2-k\,Q^2$$

A parabola fitted to the test curve; valid from shut-off to about 25 L/s.

2 · Pump curve

The twins are not quite identical

Pump curve$\Delta H=H_0\,s^2-k\,Q^2$
P-200AP-200B
Shut-off head $H_0$45.0 m46.5 m
Curve coefficient $k$0.0663 m/(L/s)²
Head at 14 L/s32.0 m33.5 m
Speed, motor3600 rpm, 10 kW

B makes 1.5 m more head, so with B running FRC-100 needs less valve opening (80 % instead of 84 %).

2 · System curve

What the pipework demandsstep 1 of 2

The pump curve is what the pump offers. The system curve is what the route from T200 to D-150 asks for.

$\Delta H = H_2 - H_1 + h_L$energy balance, T200 surface (1) to D-150 (2)
$H_1 = L_{T200}+1\ \text{m}$tank level plus 1 m to the pump centreline
$H_2 = 24\ \text{m}$D-150 at 1.5 bar g and 6 m up
$h_L$
friction and valve losses along the route
m
$L_{T200}$
liquid level in T200 (3.0 m at design)
m

2 · System curve

Losses grow with the square of flowstep 2 of 2

$h_L=(r_{line}+r_{leg}+K_{V100})\,Q^2$turbulent flow: loss ∝ velocity²
$\Delta H_{sys}=(24-4)+(0.0179+0.0026+K_{V100})\,Q^2$design level 3 m gives H₁ = 4 m
$r_{line}$
tank outlet, V200 and strainer S-200
m/(L/s)²
$r_{leg}$
suction valve, check valve and discharge valve of one pump leg
m/(L/s)²
$K_{V100}$
control valve, E-100 tubes and the line to D-150
m/(L/s)²

At 14 L/s: 20 m static + 3.5 m suction + 0.5 m leg + 8.0 m through V100 and E-100 = 32.0 m.

3 · Operating point

V100 sets the steepness of the system curve

$x$
V100 opening
0–1
$R$
rangeability of the equal-percentage trim, 30
—
$f(x)$
relative flow capacity of the trim
—
$$f(x)=\dfrac{R^{\,x}-1}{R-1}\qquad K_{V100}=0.0192+\dfrac{0.00698}{f(x)^2}$$

Each 10 % of travel multiplies capacity by about 1.4: equal percentage.

At 84 % open, K = 0.041; fully open, K = 0.026 m/(L/s)².

3 · Operating point

The pump runs where the two curves cross

Pump and system, from this part$H_0s^2-kQ^2 \;=\; (H_2-H_1)+(r_{line}+r_{leg}+K_{V100})\,Q^2$
$$Q=\sqrt{\dfrac{H_0\,s^2-(H_2-H_1)}{k+r_{line}+r_{leg}+K_{V100}}}$$
$Q=\sqrt{\dfrac{45-20}{0.0663+0.0179+0.0026+0.0408}}=14.0$ L/spump A, full speed, V100 84 %

If $H_0s^2$ falls below the static 20 m, no flow reaches D-150.

Interactive — move the operating point

Throttle, slow down, or change the static head

Closing V100 steepens the system curve; slowing the pump lowers the pump curve — the flow is wherever the two meet.

3 · Operating point

Speed changes the whole pump curve

$$\dfrac{Q_2}{Q_1}=s\qquad \dfrac{H_2}{H_1}=s^2\qquad \dfrac{P_2}{P_1}=s^3$$

Affinity laws: same impeller, similar flow pattern, speed ratio $s$.

At 1800 rpm the shut-off head is 45 × 0.25 = 11 m — below the 20 m static lift.

Speed is fixed here (3600 rpm, no variable-speed drive), so V100 is the only flow handle.

4 · Power, current, NPSH

Power and motor current

$P_{hyd}$
power given to the liquid, $\rho g Q \Delta H$
kW
$P$
shaft power from the test curve
kW
$\eta$
pump efficiency, $P_{hyd}/P$
—
$I$
motor current, read on II-210 / II-220
A
$$P=2.3\,s^3+3.42\,s^2\dfrac{Q}{14}\qquad I=5.5+1.35\,P$$

Design: 5.72 kW, 13.2 A, η 67 %. Shut-off: 2.3 kW, 8.6 A.

Interactive — slide along the pump curve

Least power at shut-off, best efficiency near 14 L/s

From the previous slide$P=2.3+3.42\,\dfrac{Q}{14}\qquad \eta=\dfrac{\rho g Q\Delta H}{P}$

Current rises with flow, so a low current means little flow and a high current means run-out — and a pump starts against a closed discharge for the smallest load.

4 · Power, current, NPSH

NPSH: how far the suction is from boiling

$\text{NPSH}_a$
net positive suction head available at the pump inlet
m
$\text{NPSH}_r$
NPSH the pump needs, from the vendor test
m
$p_v$
vapour pressure of the feed (0.3 kPa; light ends raise it)
kPa
$H_S$
suction header head, read on PI-209
m
$$\text{NPSH}_a=\dfrac{p_{atm}-p_v}{\rho g}+H_S\;>\;\text{NPSH}_r$$

Design: 12.3 m available, 4.5 m required. Below the line the pump cavitates.

Interactive — starve the suction

Where NPSH available meets NPSH required

Fouling drags PI-209 down, light ends raise $p_v$: either way the crossing moves to lower flow, and cutting the flow is the immediate cure.

5 · Two pumps in parallel

In parallel, flows add at the same head

Pump curve, per pump$\Delta H=H_0\,s^2-k\,Q^2$
$$Q_{A+B}(\Delta H)=Q_A(\Delta H)+Q_B(\Delta H)$$

Both pumps share one suction and one discharge header, so they see one ΔH.

The combined curve is wider, not taller. Against 20 m of static head a second pump adds far less than double the flow.

5 · Two pumps in parallel

The check valve keeps the idle pump from running backwards

  • The idle pump's discharge sees the full header head.
  • A seated check valve holds it back: the idle gauge reads suction head, 0.5 m.
  • Each leg keeps its own check valve and block valves, so the spare stays lined up, ready to start.

Interactive — two pumps in parallel

What one pump or two deliver as V100 opens

The second pump adds far less than its own rated flow: the static head and the friction push both pumps back up their curves.

Part 1 · summary

What Part 1 settled

  • Pumps are rated in head; 1 m of this oil is 8.53 kPa.
  • Flow sits where the pump curve meets the system curve; at design 14 L/s and 32 m.
  • V100 is the only handle: fully open, one pump gives at most 14.9 L/s.
  • Current tracks flow; NPSH available must stay above required.
  • Two pumps in parallel add flow at the same head; together they give far less than double.

2 · Required head

Where the 32 m of head goes at 14 L/s

System curve, Part 1$\Delta H_{sys}=(H_2-H_1)+(r_{line}+r_{leg}+K_{V100})\,Q^2$

Static lift takes two thirds. V100 itself takes only 4.2 m, about an eighth — that small share is all FRC-100 has to work with.

Interactive — size a pump for a new duty

From flow and lift to head, power and motor

Part 1$P=\dfrac{\rho g Q\,\Delta H}{\eta}$

Head grows with lift and with the valve's share; power grows with both flow and head — a bigger valve margin is paid for in kilowatts every hour.

2 · Pump and motor

The selected pump and its motor

QuantityValueWhy it matters
Rated point14 L/s at 32–33.5 mduty met at V100 84 %
Best-efficiency flow14.4 L/sdesign sits near it
Shaft power at design5.72 kW, η 67 %II-210 reads 13.2 A
Motor10 kW, full-load 18.9 Acovers run-out to about 25 L/s
Overload relay 4921.7 A for 10 s≈ 115 % of full-load current

3 · Control valve V100

How much flow is left in the valve?

The pump is chosen. Now the question is how far V100 can still open.

Operating point, Part 1$Q=\sqrt{\dfrac{H_0s^2-(H_2-H_1)}{k+r_{line}+r_{leg}+K_{V100}}}$
$x=0.84:\ Q=\sqrt{25/0.1276}=14.0$ L/sdesign opening
$x=1.00:\ Q=\sqrt{25/0.1128}=14.9$ L/svalve wide open, K = 0.026

Only 6 % margin: FRC-100 at 100 % output means one pump is already at its limit.

Interactive — valve opening against flow

The installed characteristic of V100

Part 1$f(x)=\dfrac{R^{x}-1}{R-1}$

Above 70 % the curve flattens: the last 16 % of travel buys under 1 L/s with one pump; a second pump lifts the whole curve.

4 · Two pumps, one spare

Two identical legs, one on standby

  • 2 × 100 %: either pump alone carries the full 14 L/s.
  • Each leg: suction valve, pump, casing gauge, check valve, discharge valve.
  • The spare stands with both block valves open, held by its check valve — ready at one button.

4 · Two pumps, one spare

Suction design: keep NPSH well above the need

FeatureDesign choiceEffect
Pump elevationtank bottom 1 m above pumpsflooded suction, self-priming
NPSH12.3 m available, 4.5 m required7.8 m margin at design
Strainer S-200common to both pumpsprotects impellers; fouls over time
T200 levelLSL 15 % permissive, LSLL 10 % tripnever uncover the tank outlet

What each trip guards against

TripSettingGuards against
LSLL-200T200 < 10 % for 5 spumps drawing air: both stop
TSHH-212 / 222casing > 110 °C for 5 srunning deadheaded or dry

5 · Protections

Why a deadheaded pump heats up

$M_c$
heat capacity of casing and trapped liquid, 20
kJ/K
$T_c$
casing temperature, TI-212 / TI-222
°C
$\dot m c_p$
heat carried away by the flow
kW/K
$$M_c\dfrac{dT_c}{dt}=(P-P_{hyd})-\dot m c_p\,(T_c-60)-0.01\,(T_c-30)$$

At shut-off all 2.3 kW becomes heat and no flow removes it: about 6 °C per minute.

Interactive — run against a closed valve

How long before TSHH-212 trips?

Previous slide$M_c\,\dot T_c=(P-P_{hyd})-\dot m c_p(T_c-60)$

With no flow TI-212 alarms at about 4.5 min and trips at about 10 min; a trickle of 0.3 L/s holds the casing well below the alarm.

Part 2 · summary

What Part 2 settled

  • 14 L/s needs 32 m: 20 m static, 7.8 m of lines and E-100, 4.2 m across V100.
  • 5.7 kW at 67 % efficiency on a 10 kW motor; 13.2 A normal, 21.7 A trips.
  • V100 at 84 % leaves only 6 % more flow on one pump.
  • 2 × 100 % pumps; the spare waits behind its check valve.
  • Every trip protects a named failure; deadheading costs about 6 °C per minute.

Part 3 · Operation

How are the pumps started, switched, run and stopped without hurting them or the cat cracker?

Part 3 · the plan

A pump's life on shift

  1. Before the startline-up, venting and the permissives
  2. Starting against a closed dischargewhy, what to read, and how long you may wait
  3. Bringing the feed on lineflow first, then steam, then AUTO
  4. Changeover and parallel runningswitching pumps without losing the feed

1 · Before the start

Line up, vent, check the permissives

  1. Suction open: V200 and the pump's suction valve (V202 for A) fully open.
  2. Vent the casing until liquid shows, then close the vent.
  3. Discharge closed: V201 shut; FRC-100 in MAN at 0–5 %.
  4. Permissives green on the SIS tab: T200 ≥ 15 %, no trip latched.

1 · Before the start

A pump full of air makes no head

  • An impeller spinning in gas lifts nothing: the gauge stays at suction head.
  • Current stays near no-load, about 6.6 A.
  • Running dry ruins the seal in about a minute.
After startVentedAir-bound
Casing gauge≈ 49 m0.5 m
Motor current8.6 A6.6 A
Vibration1.8 mm/s9 mm/s

2 · Starting

Start against a closed discharge — briefly

The pump is full and lined up. The power curve from Part 1 decides how to start it.

Power, Part 1$P=2.3\,s^3+3.42\,s^2\,\dfrac{Q}{14}\qquad I=5.5+1.35\,P$
  • With $Q=0$ the motor accelerates on its smallest load: 2.3 kW, 8.6 A.
  • Read the casing gauge: a healthy pump shows ≥ 40 m (about 49 m).
  • Open the discharge within 2 minutes — the casing heats about 6 °C per minute.

Interactive — start P-200A step by step

Virtual start-up: what each step shows

Each check has a number behind it — no head on the gauge means air, and every minute against a closed valve costs about 6 °C.

3 · Bringing the feed on line

Flow first, then steam, then AUTO

  1. FRC-100 MAN 55 %: about 9 L/s (30 % gives only 3.6 L/s).
  2. Steam on once oil flows: TIC-110 MAN about 48 %.
  3. FRC-100 AUTO at 14 L/s; cat cracker ramps its charge.
  4. Tank farm: HIC-199 70 % (14 L/s).
  5. Spare on standby; TIC-110 AUTO at 150 °C.

4 · Changeover and parallel

Changeover A → B without losing the feed

#StepWhy
1Vent B, close V205B full; least starting load
2Start B, PI-220 ≥ 40 mcatches air, rotation, blockage
3Open V205FRC-100 absorbs the bump
4Stop A, close V201no reliance on NRV-210
5Hold 5 min at 14 L/sB proven, V100 about 80 %

4 · Changeover and parallel

Running both pumps for 16 L/s

Part 1$Q_{A+B}(\Delta H)=Q_A(\Delta H)+Q_B(\Delta H)$
At 16 L/sP-200AP-200B
Flow7.3 L/s8.7 L/s
Casing gauge40.9 m40.9 m
Current11.0 A11.5 A

V100 settles at 74 %. B, the stronger pump, carries more.

Interactive — where a pump likes to run

The operating window of one pump

Below about 6 L/s the flow recirculates and vibration rises; above about 18 L/s NPSH margin and current run out — stay near 14 L/s, the best-efficiency region.

5 · Running window

What to watch while the pump runs

ReadingNormalTells you
FRC-100 output84 % (A) · 80 % (B)100 % = the pumps cannot deliver more
II-210 / II-22013.2 Alow = little flow or air; high = run-out, lost phase

5 · Shutdown

Normal shutdown: reverse the start

  1. Cat cracker takes its charge to 0 %.
  2. Steam off first: TIC-110 MAN 0 % — stagnant oil would reach 184 °C.
  3. Feed off: FRC-100 MAN 0 %, V100 closed.
  4. Close V201, then stop P-200A within 2 minutes.
  5. Tank farm: HIC-199 to 0.

5 · Emergencies

Four upsets and the first move for each

Running pump trips

Start the spare at once; FRC-100 recovers 14 L/s.

Instrument air lost

V100 and TV-110 shut: stop the pump within 2 minutes.

Cat cracker stops drawing

Cut feed and steam before D-150 reaches LSHH-150.

Anything unsafe

ESD: stops both pumps, closes V100 and TV-110.

Interactive — the D-150 clock

How much time does an upset leave you?

$$\dfrac{dL_{150}}{dt}=\dfrac{Q_{feed}-Q_{charge}}{30\ \text{m}^3}$$

$L_{150}$ in % of the 30 m³ drum: 1 %/min = 5 L/s.

A lost pump empties D-150 in about 14 minutes from 50 % — the spare must be running long before that, which is why it waits ready.

Part 3 · summary

What Part 3 settled

  • Vent, close the discharge, start, read ≥ 40 m, open within 2 minutes.
  • Flow before steam; steam off before flow stops.
  • Change over by proving the new pump before stopping the old one.
  • Current, local gauges, casing temperature and noise show pump health.
  • D-150 gives about 14 minutes when the feed is lost.

What happens to the feed between T200 and the cat cracker?

Interactive — click a block

The route from tank farm to cat cracker

Seven units in series with one pump pair in parallel — every litre the cat cracker charges has passed T200, S-200, one pump, V100 and E-100.

2 · The route

Stretch 1: tank to suction header1 of 3

The diagram named the units. Now follow the liquid through them, stretch by stretch.

  • The tank farm tops up T200 through HIC-199: 14 L/s at design, level 30 % (339 m³, 6.7 h of feed).
  • Feed leaves through V200 and strainer S-200 into the common suction header.
  • 4 m of liquid above the pumps minus 3.5 m of suction loss: PI-209 reads 0.5 m.

2 · The route

Stretch 2: pumps and discharge header2 of 3

  • P-200A runs: 32 m of head at 14 L/s, PI-210 ≈ 32.4 m, about 13 A.
  • P-200B stands by with V206 and V205 open; PI-220 ≈ 0.5 m while NRV-220 holds the header back.
  • The header low-point drain to the oily-water sewer (OWS) is normally closed.

2 · The route

Stretch 3: flow control, preheat and the drum3 of 3

  • FE-100 / FRC-100 hold the cat cracker's set point, 14 L/s, with V100 about 84 % open.
  • E-100 condenses about 4 t/h of steam at 5 bar g: feed 60 → 150 °C, 2.3 MW.
  • D-150 (30 m³) buffers the feed; the cat cracker draws 14 L/s (FI-151).

Part 4 · summary

What Part 4 settled

  • T200 → S-200 → P-200A/B → FE-100/V100 → E-100 → D-150 → cat cracker.
  • At design: 14 L/s everywhere, 0.5 m suction, 32.4 m on PI-210, 150 °C out of E-100.
  • The strainer spends head before the pump; V100 and E-100 after it.
  • Pump flow = metered flow + any flow that leaves elsewhere.

3 · The flow loop

FRC-100: measure, compare, move V100

The tags name the parts. Here they work together as one loop.

3 · The flow loop

The PI law inside FRC-100

$OP$
controller output to V100
%
$e$
error: set point − measured flow, in % of the 0–20 L/s span
%
$K_c$
controller gain, 0.35
%/%
$T_i$
integral (reset) time, 3
s
$$OP=K_c\left(e+\dfrac{1}{T_i}\int_0^t e\,dt\right)$$

Output clamped at 0–100 %: at 100 % the controller has nothing left to give.

Interactive — tune FRC-100

A set-point step on the flow loop

Previous slide$OP=K_c\left(e+\frac{1}{T_i}\int e\,dt\right)$

The installed tuning follows a step smoothly, without overshoot; a set point above 14.9 L/s saturates V100 at 100 % no matter how it is tuned.

4 · Other loops

TIC-110 and HIC-199

LoopMovesTuningNormally
TIC-110TV-110 steam to E-100 (FC)$K_c$ 1.2, $T_i$ 120 sMAN at 50 %, SP 150 °C
HIC-199tank-farm transfer to T200hand set70 % = 14 L/s

With TIC-110 in MAN the steam stays put, so less feed comes out hotter — a free flow indicator on TI-110.

4 · Fail-safe positions

When the instrument air fails

  • V100 and TV-110 are fail closed (FC): no feed, no steam.
  • The running pump is now deadheaded: PI-210 49 m, II-210 8.6 A.
  • Stop it within 2 minutes; TSHH-212 would trip it at about 10.
ValveOn air loss
V100 (feed)closes
TV-110 (steam)closes
Hand valvesstay put

Interactive — push the process towards its trips

Which trip acts, and what does it do?

Alarms warn first and trips act later — the gap between them is the operator's time to fix the cause.

5 · Rev C

The Rev C engineering upgrade

PIT-210 / PIT-220

Casing pressure on the DCS; PAH alarms when an idle casing exceeds 8 m.

MOV V201 / V205

Discharge valves that close when their pump stops.

Installed from the SIS tab by the instructor, to compare detection before and after.

Part 5 · summary

What Part 5 settled

  • A bubble without a bar is local: PI-209, PI-210, PI-220 are read only in the field.
  • FRC-100 is a PI loop ($K_c$ 0.35, $T_i$ 3 s) on a fail-closed V100.
  • TIC-110 normally sits in MAN; HIC-199 sets the tank-farm transfer.
  • Air loss shuts V100 and TV-110: stop the deadheaded pump.
  • Five trips guard the tank, casings, motors and drum; Rev C makes the idle leg visible.

Interactive — the Overview display

What each part of the Overview tells you

Tabs are the map; the Overview is where every shift starts.

Grey bubbles marked local have no value on the DCS — the three local gauges are read only in the field.

2 · Displays

Pumps display: motors, casings and the live curve

  • State, current, calculated power, casing temperature and speed of each pump.
  • A mini pump curve with FRC-100 drawn on it.
  • Reference lines: shut-off heads, design current, alarm and trip settings.

2 · Displays

Preheater and D-150 display

  • TI-110 with TIC-110 mode, TV-110, steam FI-112 and shell PI-111.
  • A heat balance: steam heat against heat taken by the feed.
  • D-150 level, feed in minus charge out, and the cat-cracker state.

2 · Displays

Energy display: what the station costs

  • Pump electric power, steam use and the cost rate in $/h.
  • Shortfall to the cat cracker is charged as lost production.
  • Used by the optimisation exercise: same feed, least energy.

3 · Faceplate

The faceplate: one loop, all its handles

  • Click a bubble on any display to open its faceplate.
  • PV (measured), SP (wanted), OUT (valve signal) as numbers and bars.
  • Manual / Automatic: in MAN you set OUT; in AUTO you set SP.
  • Tuning and alarm limits at the bottom.

3 · Trends and alarms

Trends show the story; alarms show what broke a limit

Four minutes after pump A tripped: flow and II-210 at zero, TI-110 up to 184 °C, D-150 falling; the alarm list shows the order they came in.

4 · Field

The Field tab: walk to the pumps

  • Start / stop the motors; hand valves take about 25 s full stroke.
  • Casing vents and the header drain.
  • Read PI-209, PI-210, PI-220; listen and touch for noise and rotation.
  • Phone the tank farm and the cat cracker.

4 · Pump curves

The Pump curves tab: find the flow from a gauge

  1. Read the running pump's gauge minus PI-209: its head.
  2. On its curve, that head gives the flow the pump really makes.
  3. Much more than FRC-100? The flow is going somewhere else.

5 · Safety system

The SIS tab: permissives, trips, reset

After a trip: find the cause, reset here, then restart from the Field tab with the normal checks.

What Part 6 settled

  • Operate from the DCS console; look, listen and touch on the Field tab.
  • Four displays: overview, pumps, preheater and D-150, energy.
  • A faceplate is where MAN/AUTO, SP and OUT are changed.
  • The Pump curves tab turns a gauge reading into a flow.
  • The SIS tab shows permissives, the first-out trip and the reset.

The units around the pumps

1 · T200

T200: the tank that sets the suction head

ItemValue
Size, roofØ 12 m × 10 m, cone roof, 60 °C

1 · T200

How fast T200 falls when the transfer stops

Tank balance, Part 4$A_{T200}\,\dfrac{dL}{dt}=Q_{in}-Q_{pump}$
$\dfrac{dL}{dt}=\dfrac{0-0.014}{113.1}=-1.24\times10^{-4}$ m/stransfer lost, pumps still at 14 L/s
$= -0.074$ %/min: 13 % → 10 % in about 41 minlevel in % of the 10 m shell

Cutting the feed to 10 L/s stretches this to about 57 min.

2 · S-200

S-200: the largest suction loss

  • Keeps scale and debris out of both impellers.
  • Loss grows with $Q^2$ and with fouling — up to 8 × when badly plugged.
  • The symptom is PI-209 falling, then crackle as NPSH runs out.
S-200Clean70 % plugged
PI-2090.5 m−8.3 m
Flow, V100 100 %14.9 L/s10.9 L/s
Vibration A1.8 mm/s3.4 mm/s

3 · E-100

E-100: condensing steam heats the feed

Tank and strainer shape the suction. Downstream, E-100 turns flow into temperature.

$T_s$

—
$$T_{out}=60+(T_s-60)\,\varepsilon,\qquad \varepsilon=1-e^{-UA/C}$$

Design: ε = 0.91, $T_s$ = 159 °C, so TI-110 = 150 °C.

Interactive — the preheater

What moves TI-110 when TIC-110 is in MAN

With the valve fixed, less feed comes out hotter and low steam pressure or fouling makes it colder — TI-110 is a second witness to the flow.

3 · E-100

Steam after flow, steam off before flow stops

  • With no flow the oil in the tubes creeps up to the steam temperature: about 184 °C at 11 bar a.
  • Condensate leaves through a trap; a flooded trap would cut the duty.
  • Air failure closes TV-110 (fail closed) together with V100.

4 · D-150

D-150: the buffer between two units

ItemValue
Volume, pressure, height30 m³ at 1.5 bar g, 6 m above the pumps
Design level50 % = 15 m³ = 18 min of charge at 14 L/s
AlarmsLI-150 LO 30 % · HI 80 %
TripsLSHH-150 95 % shuts V100 · LALL-150 10 % stops the charge pump

Interactive — both inventories for one hour

T200 and D-150 when flows do not match

T200 moves slowly (113 m²) and D-150 fast (30 m³) — a feed mismatch is felt at D-150 in minutes, a transfer loss at T200 in hours.

5 · The neighbours

What the tank farm and the cat cracker can do

Tank farm

Sets HIC-199 (100 % = 20 L/s) when phoned.

Cat cracker

Sends FRC-100 its remote set point and changes its charge when asked; ramps take 10 min.

Both are reached from the Field tab; every call is logged and counts in the procedures.

Part 7 · summary

What Part 7 settled

  • T200 gives the suction head and 6.7 h of feed; LSLL-200 guards its outlet.
  • S-200 is the biggest suction loss; PI-209 shows it fouling.
  • E-100: $T_{out}=60+(T_s-60)\varepsilon$; in MAN less flow means hotter oil.
  • D-150 holds about 18 minutes of charge; its level shows any feed mismatch.

Seven kinds of exercise and what each trains

ExerciseObjectiveGraded
DCS reading sheetread every key tag and its alarm limits from the DCS/15

1 · Exercise types

The four warm-ups

DCS reading sheet

Objective: know where every number lives.

Read 12 tags with their LO/HI limits; readings within ±3 %, limits within ±1 %.

What-if

Objective: predict before you act.

Choose ↑, ↓ or = for eight variables 15 min after an event, then run it.

Trend matching

Objective: recognise an upset by its shape.

Four ten-minute trends, six pens each; name the event behind each.

Scrambles

Objective: fix the order of standard jobs.

Start-up, changeover and shutdown steps shuffled; put them back.

2 · Procedures

How a procedure is graded

The warm-ups build reading skills. Procedures put them to work on a whole job.

  • The tracker ticks each step when its condition is met in the model.
  • 0 / 10 if anything unsafe happens: deadhead over 2 min, dry running, a trip, D-150 overfilled.
  • Otherwise 10, minus 4 out of order, 2 over time, 1 if the right people were not told.

2 · Procedures

Cold startup1 of 2

Objective: Start the station from cold in the right order and hand 14 L/s at 150 °C to the cat cracker.

Both pumps drained after maintenance, all block valves closed, feed stopped. Prime and start pump A, establish 14 L/s, heat the feed and hand it to the cat cracker. Limit 60 min.

  1. T200 suction lined up: V200 and V202 fully open
  2. Pump A casing vented until liquid shows at the vent, vent closed again
  3. Discharge V201 closed; FRC-100 in MAN with V100 at 5 % or less
  4. P-200A started against the closed discharge valve
  5. PI-210 read at shut-off head (≥ 40 m) before V201 is opened
  6. V201 fully open within 2 minutes of the start
  7. Flow established in MAN: V100 opened until FRC-100 reads 5 L/s or more

2 · Procedures

Cold startup2 of 2

  1. Steam on only after the flow: TV-110 opened to 20 % or more
  2. FRC-100 in AUTO at 14 L/s (±0.3)
  3. Cat cracker told the feed is ready (charge ramping up)
  4. Tank-farm transfer on: HIC-199 at 60 % or more
  5. Spare P-200B on standby: V206 open, casing vented full, vent closed, V205 closed
  6. TIC-110 in AUTO at 150 °C
  7. Hold 10 min: FRC-100 14 ±0.5 L/s, TI-110 140–160 °C, D-150 30–80 %, no alarm active or unacknowledged

2 · Procedures

Normal shutdown

Objective: Stop feed, steam and pump in order without deadheading.

The cat cracker is coming off feed. Stop the feed and pump A in an orderly way. Limit 40 min.

  1. Cat cracker told to stop drawing charge (charge to 0 %)
  2. Steam off before the flow stops: TIC-110 in MAN and TV-110 closed
  3. Feed stopped: FRC-100 in MAN and V100 closed
  4. Discharge V201 closed
  5. P-200A stopped (deadheaded no more than 2 minutes)
  6. Tank-farm transfer stopped (HIC-199 at 0)

2 · Procedures

Pump changeover A → B

Objective: Swap the running pump while the feed stays at 14 L/s.

Routine: B takes over so that A can be inspected. Keep 14 L/s throughout. Limit 30 min.

  1. B lined up: V206 open, casing vented full, vent closed
  2. V205 closed before the start
  3. P-200B started against the closed V205
  4. PI-220 read at shut-off head (≥ 40 m) with V205 still closed
  5. V205 opened fully: both pumps on the header, FRC-100 still in AUTO
  6. P-200A stopped
  7. A left on standby with its discharge closed: V201 closed
  8. Hold 5 min: FRC-100 14 ±0.3 L/s in AUTO, V100 output below 95 %, no alarm

2 · Procedures

Running pump trips

Objective: Recover the feed within 3 minutes of an unplanned pump trip.

Stand by at design. Something will happen to pump A. Limit 15 min.

  1. Trip recognised: pump A motor-trip alarm acknowledged
  2. Spare P-200B started
  3. V205 fully open with B running
  4. FRC-100 back to 14 ±0.5 L/s in AUTO
  5. Tripped pump A isolated: V201 closed
  6. Electrician and the cat cracker informed

2 · Procedures

More feed: B in parallel

Objective: Run both pumps in parallel to deliver 16 L/s.

The cat cracker wants 16 L/s: more than one pump can give through this system. Limit 40 min.

  1. B lined up: V206 open, casing vented full, vent closed
  2. P-200B started against a closed V205 and PI-220 read at shut-off (≥ 40 m)
  3. V205 opened fully: A and B in parallel
  4. FRC-100 set point raised to 16 L/s and the flow following it (±0.3)
  5. Both pumps sharing: II-210 and II-220 within 3 A of each other
  6. Hold 5 min at 16 ±0.3 L/s with no alarm

2 · Procedures

The lazy twin: unknown upset

Objective: Return pump A to service and find what stops it delivering.

B has been running for a week and is due for maintenance. Put A back in service and release B. Limit 45 min.

  1. P-200A running and P-200B stopped
  2. Idle leg tested: PI-220 read while B is idle and A runs
  3. Back-flow path closed: V205 closed with B idle
  4. FRC-100 at 14 ±0.3 L/s in AUTO with V100 output below 95 %, B idle
  5. B isolated for its maintenance: V206 closed as well
  6. Hold 5 min at 14 ±0.3 L/s with no alarm

2 · Procedures

Optimisation, 30 min

Objective: Deliver the same feed at the least energy cost.

The night shift left the station running wastefully. Find the cheapest way to deliver the same feed. Limit 30 min.

  1. FRC-100 in AUTO at 14 ±0.3 L/s
  2. TI-110 within 145–155 °C (TIC-110 in AUTO or trimmed)
  3. Pump electric power ≤ 7 kW (one pump) and steam ≤ 4.2 t/h
  4. Spare left on standby (stopped, discharge closed); no alarm active or unacknowledged

3 · Training exercises

Twenty upsets, one at a time

  • Each exercise loads its own starting state and injects one upset on a schedule.
  • In trainee mode only the situation is shown — the cause is yours to find.
  • Recovered = back in the operating band for 60 s: feed, TI-110, D-150, casings.

3 · Training exercises

Training exercises 1–3

4 · Think EQUIPPED

The six stages every case is worked through

StageObjective
1 Engagedecide: keep running, safe-park, or shut down — and why
2 Definestate the problem with numbers: what IS and IS NOT affected
3 Explorecheck readings against each other and against the curves
4 Planlist hypotheses, each with the test that would disprove it
5 Do itpredict, act, and compare the result with the prediction
6 Look backpropose a permanent fix the simulator can test

4 · Think EQUIPPED cases

Cases TE-1 and TE-2

TE-1

The lazy twin

Diagnose a flow shortfall that appears with only one pump running.

Situation: A runs, B is the spare. FRC-100 is short with its output at 100 %. Switching to B fixed it last week; B must now go to maintenance.

TE-2

Short of feed whichever pump runs

Find why the feed is short whichever pump runs.

Situation: FRC-100 has drifted low over an hour with its output at 100 %. Changing to B and back made no difference.

4 · Think EQUIPPED cases

Cases TE-3 and TE-4

TE-3

Short of feed with pump A only

Diagnose a slow decline and test the shift's first guess.

Situation: Flow has fallen for days on pump A; V100 is at 100 %. The shift suspects B's check valve.

TE-4

Pump crackles and the feed sags

Trace a noise and a sagging flow to their source and act safely.

Situation: A gravel-like noise from pump A grows louder; FRC-100 is slightly low and V100 is opening.

4 · Think EQUIPPED cases

Cases TE-5 and TE-6

TE-5

Half the feed after the electricians left

Find why a repaired pump gives half the flow.

Situation: Motor A was rewired overnight. Back on line A gives about half the feed, V100 wide open, A noisy.

TE-6

Short of feed and a smell of oil

Find a loss that no pump change cures.

Situation: FRC-100 is about 1.4 L/s low at 100 % output with either pump. Painters report oil in the gully.

4 · Think EQUIPPED cases

Cases TE-7 and TE-8

TE-7

Motor A trips again after every reset

Stop a reset-and-restart loop and find the real cause.

Situation: P-200A tripped on overload; it was reset and restarted twice and tripped within seconds each time.

TE-8

Feed cool with the steam valve wide open

Find why the feed is cool with the steam valve wide open.

Situation: TIC-110 in AUTO; TI-110 sits a few degrees under 150 °C while TV-110 has crept from 50 % to over 90 %.

4 · Think EQUIPPED cases

Cases TE-9 and TE-10

TE-9

The spare will not pump

Get a refilled spare pumping without damaging it.

Situation: B was drained and refilled after a strainer change. Change over from A to B now.

TE-10

Noisy pump since the feed tank was changed

Find the source of a pump noise that began after a tank change.

Situation: The feed source switched to T200 yesterday. A has become noisy; FRC-100 slightly low, V100 opening.

4 · Think EQUIPPED cases

Cases TE-11 and TE-12

TE-11

The lazy twin is now B

Find the cause of a flow shortfall when pump B runs alone.

Situation: A is now the spare and B runs. FRC-100 is short at 100 % output; the shift blames B.

TE-12

Short of feed, pump A gauge high

Read a high gauge together with a low flow.

Situation: FRC-100 fell with A running; PI-210 reads higher than usual and V201's handle is fully open.

The exercises at a glance

Every skill appears in a procedure, a training exercise and a case — practise it guided first, then meet it unannounced.

Interactive — how the score is built

The continuous score, one deduction at a time

score (starts at 100)

Ten minutes 3 L/s short costs less than one trip, and losing the cat cracker costs most — recover fast, but never by tripping the unit.

Part 8 · summary

What Part 8 settled

  • Warm-ups teach where numbers live; procedures teach the order of work.
  • Training exercises give one upset each; the cause stays hidden in trainee mode.
  • Think EQUIPPED cases are solved with six stages, graded on the worksheet.
  • Recover fast; a trip or a lost cat cracker costs more than a slow fix.

Closing

Key Takeaways

1

Find the flow where the pump curve meets the system curve.

2

Treat FRC-100 at 100 % output as "the pumps cannot deliver more".

3

Read both local gauges before blaming the running pump.

4

Start against a closed discharge, prove shut-off head, open within 2 minutes.

5

Check every reading against a second, independent witness.
